figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. In vitro assays to evaluate the enzymatic activity of EUGTs. (A) SDS-PAGE analysis of EUGTs purification. (B) HPLC analysis of in vitro
enzymatic reconstitution of EUGTs. (C) The conversion rate comparison of in vitro assays of EUGTs. The results are means of three independent
experiments and error bars indicate standard deviations.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Construction and productivity analysis of emodin glucoside-producing A. terreus cell factories. (A) Schematic representation of EUGT
gene integration at the H6231 chromosomal locus in the ΔgedA-ΔpyrG strain. (B) HPLC analysis of fermentation products from different EUGT
overexpression strains after 7 days of cultivation, monitored at 440 nm. Traces i and ii show authentic standards of E6G and E8G, respectively.
Strain ΔgedA-Δ6231 (trace xiii) served as a negative control. (C) Titers evaluation of E6G and E8G production by different EUGT overexpression
strains after 7 days of shake flask fermentation. Product titers were determined by HPLC peak area analysis. Data are presented as mean ± SD from
three independent biological replicates.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Evaluation of fusion protein strategies to address bottlenecks in emodin glucoside production. (A) Scheme of the challenges in emodin
glucoside production. (B) Schematic representation of the fusion protein design and chromosomal integration strategy. Top: The double mutant
GedAM protein lost its ability to convert emodin to questin. Bottom: Schematic illustration of various fusion protein configurations combining
GedAM, OsUGT, and GFP domains with different linkers. Right: Integration of the fusion constructs at the H6231 locus in the ΔgedA-ΔpyrG
strain. (C) HPLC analysis of emodin glucoside production in strains expressing different fusion protein variants after 7-day fermentation (λ = 440
nm). Traces i and ii show authentic standards of E6G and E8G, respectively. (D) Fluorescence microscopy analysis of protein expression and
subcellular distribution of different fusion protein variants. Merge: Merge-field images. All scale bars represent 10 μm.

Figure 4. Emodin glucoside production by whole-cell catalysis. (A)
HPLC analysis of emodin glucoside production catalyzed by E. coli

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Predicted structures and phylogenetic analysis of EUGTs. (A) Structural superposition of OsUGT and Ft73BE, highlighting the
conserved catalytic His-Asp dyad and ligands. Yellow sticks represent amino acids and ligands in Ft73BE, while pink sticks show those from
OsUGT. N-terminal domains are colored orange (OsUGT) and wheat (Ft73BE); C-terminal domains are green (OsUGT) and cyan (Ft73BE).
(B) Comparison of key conserved amino acid residues in the emodin binding sites. Binding residues and emodin are shown as pink/cyan for
OsUGT and yellow/green for Ft73BE, respectively. Key amino acid residues involved in substrate recognition are labeled, with red and black text
indicating residues from OsUGT and Ft73BE, respectively. (C) Detailed view of OsUGT binding pocket showing residues (pink sticks) within 4Å
of the substrate emodin (cyan). The protein backbone is represented as a cyan cartoon. The red text highlights specific residues that may enable
OsUGT to catalyze C8 hydroxyl glucosylation. (D) Phylogenetic tree of EUGTs with bootstrap values (%) at branch points and scale bar
indicating 0.2 amino acid substitutions per site. OsUGT (UGT707A2) and Ft73BE (UGT73BE5) are highlighted with red dots. UGTs from
various plant species are labeled by their article designations, followed by the official nomenclature from the UGT Nomenclature Committee in
parentheses.
